summary: Defines circuit breakers for unicast RTP sessions, which stop media flows that suffer persistent heavy loss or congestion so they do not harm the network.

plainLanguage.summary: A fuse that cuts off a call stream if it keeps causing trouble, like a house fuse.

questions: what is an rtp circuit breaker
when must an rtp sender stop sending
how does rtp compare itself to tcp throughput
what is media timeout in rtp
subtitle: Four last-resort safety switches that tell an RTP sender to stop when its media flow is hurting the network.

tldr.problem: Voice and video over RTP often run on best-effort UDP networks with no standard congestion control, so a sender that never slows down can cause persistent congestion.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four RTP circuit breakers, driven by basic RTCP reports, that make a sender stop when feedback disappears, media stops arriving, loss is far worse than TCP would tolerate, or the media is unusable.
tldr.outcome: It is a protection of last resort, not a congestion control algorithm. Any Standards Track RTP congestion control must operate within its envelope.

facts.label: RTCP timeout
facts.value: At least 3 times Td, with Tmin=5 seconds

facts.label: Td and T_rr_interval caps
facts.value: Td no more than 5 s, T_rr_interval no more than 4 s

today: RFC 8083 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3550. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. The text expects a future replacement to give guidance on how ECN feedback should affect the congestion breaker.

sections.title: Why RTP Needs Circuit Breakers
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) is widely used for voice over IP, video conferencing and telepresence, often over best-effort UDP/IP networks. Without congestion control, network congestion leads to uncontrolled packet loss and a worse experience. There is no consensus on one standard congestion control algorithm for interactive RTP flows, and this memo does not propose one.

Instead it defines a minimal set of RTP circuit breakers: conditions under which there is general agreement that serious congestion is occurring and the sender needs to stop. They are a specific instance of the network transport circuit breakers of RFC 8084 and act as a protection of last resort against persistent excessive congestion. Applications on best-effort networks are expected to run without triggering them unless congestion is long-lived and excessive.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules do not teach a call how to share the road politely. They only say when the call must pull over because it is blocking everyone.

sections.title: Unicast Congestion Control Background
sections.content:
The scope is unicast RTP, one sender and one receiver. Multicast needs different solutions and is out of scope. Congestion control can live in a congestion-controlled transport such as TCP, which is safe for the network and not considered further, or in the application on top of UDP using RTCP feedback. This memo targets the second case.

Congestion can be detected through rising one-way delay, through ECN Congestion Experienced marks, or, in the extreme case, through packet loss seen as gaps in RTP sequence numbers. The receiver then reports back. Basic RTCP Receiver Reports carry the fraction of packets lost, the cumulative loss, the highest sequence number received and jitter, and let the sender estimate round-trip time, but a report cannot be sent early when congestion starts mid-interval. RTCP Extended Reports add richer metrics without changing timing. The RTP/AVPF profile allows early reports, and ECN feedback for RTP builds on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver sends back little report cards saying how many packets arrived. The report cards come only every few seconds, so the sender has to be patient and careful.

sections.title: The Variables Used
sections.content:
The circuit breakers are defined with a handful of variables. The main ones are:

  • Td: the deterministic RTCP reporting interval from RFC 3550. Tdr is the sender's estimate of that interval as calculated by the receiver of its media.
  • Tr: the round-trip time, smoothed as Tr = (0.8 * Tr) + (0.2 * Tr_new).
  • Tf: the media framing interval, and G: the number of frames coded together at one sending rate setting.
  • k: the non-reporting threshold.
  • X: the throughput a TCP connection would achieve, with s the RTP packet size, p the loss event rate, t_RTO the TCP retransmission timeout (approximated as 4 * Tr) and b the packets acknowledged per TCP acknowledgement (b = 1 is RECOMMENDED).
  • T_rr_interval: the minimal interval between RTCP reports under RTP/AVPF.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the measuring sticks: how often the report cards arrive, how long a message takes to go there and back, and how fast a polite TCP download would go on the same road.

sections.title: The Four Circuit Breakers
sections.content:
The design uses only basic RTCP features, so it works for every unicast RTP application without extended reports or rapid feedback. Implementations that sometimes talk to endpoints without RTCP need to disable the breakers unless signaling confirms the peer implements RTCP, but the RFC says they SHOULD NOT be disabled on networks that might be congested unless an equivalent mechanism exists. Round-trip time alone and jitter alone are judged too weak to serve as breakers, so the breakers rest on loss and connectivity signals.

#1 RTCP timeout. If a sender has received no RTCP SR or RR for its SSRC for at least three times Td (computed without randomization and with the fixed minimum interval of Tmin=5 seconds), it SHOULD cease transmission, because it cannot know whether it is causing congestion. Implementations SHOULD NOT configure Td above 5 seconds or T_rr_interval above 4 seconds.

#2 Media timeout. If reports show a non-increasing extended highest sequence number received, the media is not arriving. MEDIA_TIMEOUT consecutive such reports trigger the breaker, and the sender SHOULD then cease transmission. The RECOMMENDED value for k is 5 reports.

#4 Media usability. If reported loss or latency leaves the media unusable for a significant time, the sender SHOULD stop, and receivers SHOULD terminate the session. The RFC deliberately sets no bound, since this depends on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four trip wires. One trips when the report cards stop coming, one when the packets stop arriving, one when too many are being lost, and one when the call is too broken to be useful.

sections.title: The Congestion Breaker Algorithm
sections.content:
Breaker #3 compares the sender's rate with what TCP would get. The RTP/AVP profile already says RTP loss is acceptable if a TCP flow in the same conditions would get an average throughput not less than the RTP flow's, and the comparison is an order of magnitude (a factor of about ten). TCP throughput X is estimated from s, Tr and the loss rate. The RFC RECOMMENDS the simplified equation. Implementations that want more sensitivity MAY use the full equation, which tended to trigger earlier in the measurements it cites, including on LTE.

RTCP reports give the loss fraction, not the loss event rate, so the fraction is used in its place; the RFC argues this is acceptable for an order-of-magnitude test. A sender sending at least one packet every max(Tdr, Tr) seconds averages the fraction lost over the last CB_INTERVAL reporting intervals, weighted by interval duration. If its actual sending rate is more than 10 * X, the breaker triggers.

On triggering, the sender SHOULD cease transmission. It MAY first cut its rate by about a factor of ten, such as a video system dropping to audio only. If the breaker triggers again after the next CB_INTERVAL intervals, it MUST stop. When reports are sent round-robin across many sources, priority SHOULD go to reports on sources with high loss, which is an update to RFC 3550.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender asks what speed a well-behaved TCP download would reach on the same road. If the call is going more than ten times faster than that and losing packets, the fuse trips.

sections.title: Ceasing and Restarting Transmission
sections.content:
What it means to cease transmission depends on the application. It can mean stopping one RTP flow or several bundled flows on a particular 5-tuple of transport protocol, ports and IP addresses, until the network problem has dissipated. Halted flows SHOULD NOT restart automatically unless the sender has information that the congestion has cleared. Examples are a competing flow finishing or a mobile device moving to a new location. Ideally a human user decides whether to try again, which avoids automatic redial systems congesting the network.

If an implementation cannot tell whether a restart was human or scripted, it MUST rate limit restarts on the same 5-tuple so that the reaction lasts at least the triggering interval. The RFC also suggests that applications may show a user interface cue that problems are occurring before the breaker triggers.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the fuse trips, you do not flip it back on again and again. You wait until the problem is likely gone, and it is best if a person decides.

sections.title: Feedback Profiles, XR, ECN and Layers
sections.content:
With the RTP/AVPF and RTP/SAVPF profiles, reduced-size RTCP reports without an SR or RR MUST be ignored by the congestion breaker but MUST count as received packets for the RTCP timeout breaker. Reduced-size reports that do include an SR or RR are processed like regular reports, which can make the breaker trigger earlier. If T_rr_interval reduces regular reporting, Tdr in the interval formula is replaced by max(T_rr_interval, Tdr).

RTCP Extended Report blocks do not change the algorithm, except that ECN Summary Reports are used. ECN does not affect the timeout breakers, and the RFC says there is no consensus yet on how ECN feedback should affect the congestion breaker.

The breaker works per RTP session. Within a session each SSRC is treated independently by default, but a sender MAY group streams, such as the layers of a layered codec, so one trigger applies to the group, letting enhancement layers stop first. Streams with different DSCP values SHOULD NOT be grouped.
sections.plainLanguage: Quick short notes are fine and do not trip the fuse. If a call sends several video qualities at once, they can share one fuse so the extra detail switches off first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550 apply, plus those of RFC 4585 and RFC 6679 when rapid feedback or ECN feedback is used. With unauthenticated RTCP, an on-path attacker can trivially forge reports showing high loss and trigger the breaker, disrupting the session. An off-path attacker must guess the random SSRC and sequence number. Authenticating RTCP avoids the attack; options are discussed in RFC 7201.

A very long RTCP reporting interval, many minutes, can effectively disable the circuit breaker, so implementations are expected to cap the reporting interval they negotiate.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could send fake report cards to trip the fuse. Signing the report cards stops that.

cells: No SR or RR received for at least 3 times Td
MEDIA_TIMEOUT consecutive reports with non-increasing highest sequence number
Sending rate more than 10 * X over CB_INTERVAL reports
SHOULD cease; MAY first cut the rate about tenfold
Loss or latency leaves media unusable for a significant time

data.title: Timeout and throughput formulas
data.code:
MEDIA_TIMEOUT = ceil(k * max(Tf, Tr, Tdr) / Tdr)

Simplified TCP throughput (bytes per second):
  X = s / (Tr * sqrt(2*b*p/3))

Congestion breaker triggers when:
  sending rate > 10 * X
